title: Numbers and telling time
goal: Count to a thousand, tell the time the way Swedes do, and never again misunderstand the word *halv* — which means the opposite of what an English speaker expects.
bekal: the numbers 0-1000 and their ordinal forms
asking about departure times and making arrangements

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På Centralstationen
dialogs.intro: Friday morning. Dian and Oskar are standing in front of the departures board at Stockholm Central Station. They're heading to Uppsala.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Excuse me, what time is it?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Och när går tåget till Uppsala?
lines.id: And when does the train to Uppsala leave?
lines.literal: and when goes train-the to Uppsala?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Halv nio. Vi har femton minuter.
lines.id: Half past eight. We've got fifteen minutes.
lines.literal: half nine. we have fifteen minutes.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Halv nio? Alltså klockan nio och trettio?
lines.literal: half nine? so clock-the nine and thirty?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Nej! Halv nio betyder åtta trettio. Vi säger halva timmen framåt.
lines.id: No! Halv nio means eight thirty. We count the half hour forward.
lines.literal: no! half nine means eight thirty. we say half hour-the forward.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Oj. Då har vi bara femton minuter, inte fyrtiofem.
lines.id: Oops. Then we only have fifteen minutes, not forty-five.
lines.literal: oops. then have we only fifteen minutes, not forty-five.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Precis. Vilket spår? Spår sex, tror jag.
lines.id: Exactly. Which platform? Platform six, I think.
lines.literal: exactly. which track? track six, believe I.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Nittiofem kronor. Eller hundra tio om du köper ombord.
lines.id: Ninety-five kronor. Or a hundred and ten if you buy it on board.
lines.literal: ninety-five kronor. or hundred ten if you buy on-board.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Då köper jag nu. Och vi ses vid spår sex om tio minuter.
lines.id: Then I'll buy one now. See you at platform six in ten minutes.
lines.literal: then buy I now. and we see-each-other at track six in ten minutes.

notes: **Halv nio means 8:30, not 9:30.** This is the most expensive misunderstanding a newcomer to Sweden can make, and it makes people miss trains every week. British speakers are especially at risk, because British "half nine" means 9:30 — the exact opposite. Swedish — along with German, Dutch, Danish and Norwegian — counts the half hour **toward** the next hour, not **after** the current one. *Halv nio* = "half way to nine". When in doubt, double-check with numbers: *Alltså åtta trettio?*

**Klockan** (the clock) is often shortened to **klockan är** or even **den är**. Three equally correct ways to ask: *Vad är klockan?*, *Hur mycket är klockan?* and, most casually, *Vet du vad klockan är?*

**Vilket spår?** — "which platform?". *Vilken* is used with *en*-words, *vilket* with *ett*-words, *vilka* with plurals. Since it's *ett spår*, the form is *vilket*. It's the same pattern as adjectives: a *-t* ending for *ett*-words.

**Hundra tio** is written as two words, but **nittiofem** as one. The rule: numbers under a hundred are written as a single word (*tjugoett*, *fyrtiofem*, *nittionio*), while hundreds and thousands may be split. In practice, Swedes just write the digits.

**Om tio minuter** means "**in** ten minutes", pointing forward in time. Don't confuse it with *i tio minuter*, which means "**for** ten minutes". *Jag kommer om tio minuter* (I'll be there in ten minutes) is very different from *jag väntar i tio minuter* (I'm waiting for ten minutes). English learners slip here because *i* looks like "in" — but for time, Swedish "in" is *om*.

**Kronor** is the plural of *en krona*, the Swedish currency. In conversation people say *spänn* or *kronor*; prices are written "95 kr". One krona is roughly a tenth of a US dollar, so knock a zero off to get a quick feel for prices.

grammars.title: Numbers 0-20, then the tens
after: The final **-o** of the tens (*trettio*, *fyrtio*, *sjuttio*) is almost always silent in speech: **TRET-tee**, **FÖR-tee**, **HWÜT-tee**. Pronouncing it in full sounds like someone reading out a document.

The number **1** has two forms that follow the gender of the noun: *ett hus* but *en bok*. When the number stands alone — counting, phone numbers, scores — it's always **ett**: "one, two, three" is *ett, två, tre*.

**Sju (7)** and **sjuttio (70)** both use the breathy back sound: **hwü** and **HWÜT-tee**. Practice them together with *sjutton* (17), because these three sound alike to a beginner's ear and get mixed up when you're hearing prices.

grammars.title: Telling the time
after: Look at the two rows that sound strangest to an English ear: **fem i halv nio** (8:25) and **fem över halv nio** (8:35). Swedish treats the half hour as **a landmark of its own**, then counts forward and back from it. English stops at "twenty-five past" and "twenty-five to"; Swedish reaches for *halv* instead.

For official timetables — trains, flights, opening hours — Swedes use **the 24-hour clock and plain numbers**: *tåget går 14.37* is read *fjorton trettiosju*. So if *halv* ever confuses you, you can always say the raw numbers, and it still sounds perfectly natural.
**Klockan** is shortened to **kl.** in writing. To ask about an appointment: *Hur dags?* ("what time?") — shorter and more casual than *vilken tid*.

blocks.text: Month names are **not capitalized**, just like the days of the week — a small trap for English speakers, who capitalize both. Dates use ordinal numbers: *den första januari* (January 1st), *den tjugofjärde december* (December 24th). In everyday writing, *1 januari* or *2026-01-01* is enough — Sweden writes dates year-month-day, which is even the official ISO standard. No more guessing whether 03/04 is March or April.

From eleven on, the ordinal just adds **-de** or **-e**: *elfte*, *tolfte*, *trettonde*, *tjugonde*, *trettiofemte*. Only the first ten need memorizing on their own — and three of them (*första*, *andra*, *tredje*) work just like English *first*, *second*, *third*, which are irregular in exactly the same way. *Fjärde*, *femte*, *sjätte* even sound like "fourth", "fifth", "sixth".

blocks.title: Seasons, and why Swedes never stop talking about them
items: "In summer" = *på sommaren*; "this summer" = *i sommar*. Same pattern as *på kvällen* and *ikväll*.
In Stockholm the sun sets at 2:50 p.m. in December and at 10:10 p.m. in June. That's why weather and light are the number-one conversation opener in Sweden, far ahead of work or family.

blocks.text: Swedish phone numbers are read **in pairs**, not digit by digit: *45* is *fyrtiofem*, not *fyra fem*. To a beginner it sounds very fast. Your lifeline: *Kan du säga siffra för siffra?* — "could you say it one digit at a time?"

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 4
items: Cover the Swedish column in the house table in Unit 4 and say the **definite** forms from memory: the house, the kitchen, the door, the window.
Then combine them with this unit's numbers: *tre hus*, *två dörrar*, *fem fönster*, *tio rum*. Notice which ones change and which don't.
Finally, say these three times out loud: 07.15, 09.30, 17.45 — in Swedish, without looking at the table.
